The most informative experimental sections should be the requested-vs-delivered difficulty analysis, solver difficulty curves, and the SFT-versus-RL gain breakdown.4a:T813,方法上有两个核心动作。第一是目标构造。作者没有直接沿用父 subword tokenizer 的所有切分，而是围绕 grapheme cluster 设计了两类监督：一种是 every-cluster target，即保留每个 grapheme 边界；另一种是 retained-parent target，即只保留那些本来就与 grapheme 边界重合的父 tokenizer 切分。这样做的原因很明确：grapheme 边界是跨编码可表示的、对 span-preserving edit 稳定，而且正好能把“编码是否在首符号暴露了 cluster continuation 所需信息”这个问题单独拎出来。第二是编码设计与对照。作者采用已有的 UBE（Universal Byte-Level Encoding）：对 1-byte 和 2-byte UTF-8 标量保持不变，对更长的标量改写成 UTF-16 little-endian 的两个字节。这样对原本需要 3-byte UTF-8 的 codepoint，首个符号从 UTF-8 的‘4 个高位 + 长度前缀’变成了‘8 个低位’，在同一 256-codepoint page 内通常足以直接区分具体字符。为了把“更短序列”与“字节顺序”拆开，作者又构造了 UBE-BE：路由方式和总长度与 UBE 相同，但把 UTF-16 code unit 内部字节顺序反过来。这样如果 UBE 好、UBE-BE 不好，就能说明收益不是简单来自 stream 变短，而是来自 low byte first 让判别信息更早出现。

实验对象是小型 causal boundary predictor，在 matched FineWeb-2 文本上训练，在 FLORES-200 的多语种面板上评估。作者把错误分成 scalar ends 上的平衡误差，以及 scalar 内部的 false cuts；后者可以用规则 mask 去掉，不改变 scalar end 的判定，因此主分析集中在真正有意义的边界决策上。论文还构造了一个很强的诊断实验：找出那些左上下文完全相同、下一个 scalar 落在同一 256-codepoint page、但边界决策相反的成对样本。对这类样本，若编码首符号不携带足够信息，模型再怎么学也无法在一符号 lookahead 下全对；这使得“可学性”与“表示可区分性”被清楚地分开了。4b:T773,最关键的结果有三组。第一，在 17 种语言的 FLORES-200 面板上，针对 every-cluster target、只允许 one-symbol lookahead 时，UTF-8 在 scalar ends 上的 balanced error 是 8.76%，UBE 降到 0.06%，而同长度控制 UBE-BE 仍有 8.62%。这个结果很硬，因为它几乎直接说明收益来自字节顺序，而不是仅仅因为 UBE 把 3-byte UTF-8 压成了 2 个符号。第二，在作者构造的 17,204 对“相同左上下文但应作相反决策”的样本上，UBE 的训练后预测器在每个 seed 都能全部答对；UTF-8 和 UBE-BE 做不到，因为两者在关键位置看到的首符号相同，信息先天不足。第三，在 Korean 和 Chinese 这类 grapheme 边界基本等于 scalar end 的语言里，问题不再是 cluster continuation，而是 retained-parent task 中“哪些字符边界要保留为 subword 边界”。在 one-symbol lookahead 下，UBE 相对 UTF-8 的总 retained-parent error 分别下降 72.91% 和 35.29%；在另外 8 个脚本上，下降幅度在 67.32% 到 99.55% 之间。作者还指出，当某脚本主要 Unicode block 落在单一 256-codepoint page 内时，UBE-BE 与 UTF-8 会比较接近，这与“low byte first 在页内直接暴露字符身份”的机制一致。

另一个很有价值的部分是对已发布 byteification 模型的审计。作者检查了 Bwen-8B（Qwen3-8B-Base 的 Bolmo-style 转换），发现它在 18 个高碎片化语言里至少保留了 97.07% 的父模型内部切分，cluster-internal cut 数量与父 tokenizer 相差不超过 1.54%。这说明现有 byteification 流程虽然去掉了显式 tokenizer 接口，但切分偏好几乎原样继承，cluster 内部碎裂并没有真正解决。论文据此论证：如果先删除 cluster-internal cuts，再训练边界预测器，监督会更干净，也更符合 byte-level 接口想要达到的语言无关性。4c:T7be,The paper has two main technical components. The first is target construction. Instead of inheriting all parent tokenizer boundaries, the authors define grapheme-aware supervision in two forms: an every-cluster target that keeps every grapheme boundary, and a retained-parent target that keeps only those parent-tokenizer cuts already aligned with grapheme boundaries. Grapheme clusters are chosen because their boundaries are representable across encodings, stable under span-preserving edits, and directly isolate the continuation-vs-new-cluster distinction that encoding order can obscure.

The second component is the encoding comparison. The paper uses Universal Byte-Level Encoding (UBE), which keeps one- and two-byte UTF-8 encodings unchanged but rewrites longer scalars as UTF-16 little-endian bytes. For codepoints that would take three bytes in UTF-8, UBE shortens them to two symbols and, more importantly, exposes the low byte first. Within a known 256-codepoint page, that first symbol often identifies the codepoint directly. To separate stream-length effects from byte-order effects, the authors introduce UBE-BE, a big-endian control with the same routing and stream length as UBE but reversed byte order inside each UTF-16 code unit. This is a strong control: if UBE wins over both UTF-8 and UBE-BE, the gain cannot be explained by shorter streams alone.

They train small causal boundary predictors on matched FineWeb-2 text and evaluate on a multilingual FLORES-200 panel. Errors are split into scalar-end decisions and false cuts inside scalars; the latter can be removed by a rule-based mask without affecting scalar-end decisions. A particularly clean diagnostic is the constructed-pair test: pairs with identical left context, next scalars on the same 256-codepoint page, but opposite correct boundary decisions. On such pairs, failure is not about optimization difficulty. It is about whether the encoding exposes enough information at one-symbol lookahead.4d:T6ed,Three results carry most of the paper. First, on the 17-language FLORES-200 panel for the every-cluster target with one-symbol lookahead, UTF-8 yields 8.76% balanced error at scalar ends, UBE drops this to 0.06%, while UBE-BE remains at 8.62%. This is the clearest evidence that byte order, not just shorter streams, drives the improvement. Second, on 17,204 constructed pairs with identical left context but opposite correct decisions, the trained UBE predictors solve all pairs correctly for every seed. UTF-8 and UBE-BE cannot, because both expose the same first symbol at the critical position. That turns the argument from empirical correlation into representational necessity.

Third, the paper examines Korean and Chinese, where evaluated grapheme clusters are single scalars, so the task becomes subword-boundary selection rather than grapheme continuation. Even there, UBE reduces total retained-parent errors by 72.91% and 35.29% relative to UTF-8 at one-symbol lookahead. Across eight additional scripts, reductions range from 67.32% to 99.55%. The paper also notes a useful nuance: when a script’s main Unicode block lies within a single 256-codepoint page, UBE-BE stays close to UTF-8, consistent with the mechanism that low-byte-first matters most when it reveals within-page identity early.

The audit of released byteification models is also important. For Bwen-8B, a Bolmo-style conversion of Qwen3-8B-Base, at least 97.07% of the parent model’s interior cuts are retained in each of 18 high-fragmentation languages, and the grapheme-internal cut count stays within 1.54% of the parent tokenizer. Trust emits the current evaluator-preferred answer, fallback emits a conservative answer that avoids further continuation, and expand buys one more unit of inference before the controller acts again. The same framework covers both width expansion and revision expansion.
For terminal actions, the target value is success probability minus compute cost. For expand, the ideal target is the Bellman continuation value. In practice, the system learns one confidence head per action: trust and fallback estimate terminal answer success, while expand estimates a rollout-based continuation-success surrogate. These predictions are then post-hoc calibrated, and an optional uncertainty penalty is applied near brittle decision boundaries. The theory gives two main results: local action selection is stable when score error is smaller than the compute-adjusted action gap, and regret accumulates along the realized expansion path. A notable design choice is that the expand head predicts a success-based surrogate rather than the full downstream-cost-aware Bellman value, which keeps the controller lightweight.50:T425,The setup fixes K language models. The target is clean risk: over the population of questions, the gold answer must be the unique mode of the infinite-generation mixture distribution. Since the p_i are unknown, the learner observes N sampled answers from each model on each of Q labeled questions. A zero-buffer ERM can overfit finite-N noise: an empirical margin may be positive even when the true clean margin is non-positive. The proposed buffered ERM counts a question as solved only when the empirical margin exceeds a positive threshold epsilon. The audit may adaptively choose questions, extend answer paths, query correctness labels, and stop when it can return a simultaneous confidence band with half-width ε and failure probability δ. The analysis counts three resources: generated answers, correctness queries, and question visits. For a fixed list, the main cost law for certifying all budgets up to K is, up to logarithmic factors, K/ε + min(M, ε^{-2}) + s/ε^2. The three terms correspond to rare high-scoring answers at large budgets, the identity of the benchmark questions, and within-question variance accumulated along the curve. Matching lower bounds show that these terms are intrinsic. A key technical device is a coupling of nested winners on one answer path, which lets a single path serve all budgets. Combined with a multilevel audit, it attains near-minimax cost.55:T45b,The empirical study uses 185 held-out score pools. A cost law fitted before a new study predicts that study’s bill within 0.6%.56:T641,The core idea is a spatial compiler that turns rendered visual experience into dense, linked supervision. Starting from static 3D scenes and camera trajectories, the system renders RGB observation sequences. During data construction, it also has access to privileged information such as camera poses, scene geometry, and object identities. These are never exposed to the model at inference time, but they are used to compile supervision.

The supervision is organized into three connected capabilities within the same episode. First, self-motion tracking asks the model to infer how the observer moved between observations. The important point is that motion is not treated as an isolated target; it is the mechanism that should drive state updates. Second, persistent object mapping requires the model to maintain object locations and relations as the viewpoint changes, including when objects become occluded or leave the field of view. Third, operations over state ask downstream spatial questions on top of the updated internal state.

A second important design choice is motif-driven trajectory rendering. Instead of random camera paths, the authors define trajectory motifs that control how visibility, evidence, and viewpoint changes unfold over time. This lets them systematically generate episodes that require memory, re-localization, reference-frame handling, and state maintenance. The resulting questions are grouped into shared episodes so that motion estimation, state update, and reasoning are learned as connected parts of one experience rather than as unrelated instruction examples.57:T569,The paper builds Uruqi-600k and trains URUQI Syn-8B. First, it builds self-explored priors by traversing interactive elements on real devices, constructing a deduplicated UI transition graph, and using a multimodal annotator to synthesize task-trajectory pairs from reachable paths. Second, it creates drift-aware perturbations. The drift taxonomy comes from comparing old and new app versions and includes step insertion or deletion, entry-point and path shifts, control renaming, goal-mismatched detours, and distracting alternatives. Perturbation operators transform clean priors into a distribution that approximates deployment-time retrieval noise, with deterministic reliability labels. Third, it trains a reliability-gated policy. The policy first predicts a reliability variable r in {Follow, Partial, Ignore}, then generates the action conditioned on that decision: p(a|·)=Σr p(r|·)p(a|·,r). This factorization makes the agent explicitly check whether the retrieved path matches the current goal and state before acting, rather than blindly conditioning on retrieved trajectories.59:T7c5,The formulation starts from minimum-token segmentation with a vocabulary budget. Each document is represented as a byte-level DAG whose edges are candidate substring occurrences. Byte edges are always available; multibyte edges are available only if the corresponding string is selected into the vocabulary. Given a vocabulary, minimum-count encoding is just a shortest path in the usable subgraph. The coupling difficulty is that selecting one token type enables all of its occurrences across the corpus.

The main idea is an occurrence-level Lagrangian relaxation. Each candidate occurrence gets a non-negative price lambda_e. On the document side, segmentation becomes a shortest-path problem with edge costs increased by these prices. On the vocabulary side, each token type accumulates the total bid of all its priced occurrences, and the lower bound subtracts the sum of the top-K bids allowed by the vocabulary budget. This yields a computable lower bound without a generic LP solver: shortest paths per document plus a global top-K selection over token bids. The paper argues that maximizing over prices recovers the LP relaxation, while validity of the reported bound is checked separately with an exact integer checker.

A useful extension is the boundary-licence formulation. Instead of only comparing the two endpoints—fully regex-constrained versus fully unrestricted—the method allows a budget on how many vocabulary entries may cross regex cuts. That produces a compression frontier and makes the design question continuous: how much compression can be recovered by permitting a small number of cross-boundary tokens.

The paper also keeps compression and prediction separate. Compression is analyzed through certified token-count intervals. Prediction is evaluated on held-out data with an explicit vocabulary and decoding protocol, because unrestricted vocabularies change token frequencies, context granularity, and effective predictability, not just sequence length.5a:T52e,The headline result on English Wikipedia is a certified boundary tax: regex boundaries increase the optimal token count by 28.3% to 36.8%. That is a large effect, showing that pre-tokenization boundaries materially constrain the compression optimum. BPE is only 2.1% above the constrained lower bound, which supports the claim that under a fixed regex regime BPE is already close to the best achievable compression. But BPE is 10.9% above the unrestricted lower bound, which explains why boundary-relaxing methods can still obtain substantially shorter sequences. These are not contradictory findings; they refer to different optimization problems.

The multilingual study covers 12 languages. Unrestricted fitted dictionaries compress better, but they have higher mean test bits-per-byte in every language. With independent tuning and evaluation seeds, the direction remains in 11 of 12 languages. This is the most practically relevant result for LM researchers: fewer tokens do not necessarily mean easier prediction or lower held-out loss.

The boundary-licence experiments are also important, even if the abstract only hints at them. They show how compression improves as a limited number of cross-boundary vocabulary entries are allowed, which is more informative than a binary constrained-versus-unrestricted comparison.5b:T5de,RLTL;DR has two components. The first changes rollout collection. Instead of K independent parallel attempts, the agent solves the same task sequentially. After each failed attempt, the verifier is run and exposes error messages, failed assertions, tracebacks, or final-state checks. The same policy then reads the failed attempt and verifier output and writes a short TL;DR insight, such as a reminder to paginate search results. The next attempt is conditioned on the original task plus the accumulated insights. This converts some tasks from a zero-success sampling regime into a regime where at least one successful trajectory can be found.

The second component changes optimization. Sequential exploration alone does not solve test-time performance, because evaluation requires a first-attempt solution without any accumulated insights in context. The paper therefore enables backpropagation through the in-context insight tokens, about 17 tokens per insight. These insights are inserted as user messages, but their tokens receive an SFT-style loss. The policy thus internalizes a mapping from task descriptions to high-level reminders. GRPO can still be applied to rollout action tokens with a clipped objective, using epsilon 0.2, but the ablations show that the insight-token loss is the dominant source of improvement. This distinguishes the method from ordinary reflection prompting: the reflection is not only used at inference or sampling time; it is made into a parameter-learning target.5c:T4f3,The experiments use Qwen 3.5 9B Thinking as the base agent on verifiable agentic and coding tasks. Episodes allow up to 50 actions, and the verifier returns a binary reward together with rich failure observations. The selected tasks are intentionally difficult: the base policy often fails even after 128 attempts. In this regime, standard GRPO stays nearly flat, with Pass@1 around 0% to 1%.

Sequential sampling improves exploration. On tasks where independent attempts do not produce useful successes, conditioning later attempts on self-generated TL;DR insights yields Pass@k in the 14% to 59% range. However, if insights are only used during sampling and not learned into the model, evaluation without insights remains close to the original policy.

With the full RLTL;DR training procedure, evaluation is done without insights and without sequential sampling. The model must solve the task on the first attempt. Pass@1 reaches 11% to 14%, while GRPO remains at 0% to 1%. The strongest ablation disables the GRPO loss and keeps only the SFT loss on insight tokens; this recovers most of the full method’s performance. That result indicates that parameterizing the task-to-insight mapping, rather than reinforcing final rollout tokens, is the central mechanism.5d:T481,Read the Introduction and Methods closely. The Introduction gives the key failure condition for RLVR: the verifier may be correct, but the policy never reaches a successful trajectory, so there is no useful learning signal. That masking detail is the core implementation choice.

For experiments, prioritize three results: the Pass@k gain from sequential sampling, the insight-free Pass@1 evaluation, and the ablation that removes GRPO while keeping insight-token supervision. Two issues are worth deeper inspection. First, insight quality: the same policy writes the insights, so incorrect or over-specific lessons may be learned. Second, distributional reuse: the method should work best when hard tasks share recurring failure patterns. If each task requires a unique insight, the task-to-insight mapping may generalize less reliably.5e:T4e8,The paper uses Partial Information Decomposition to separate multimodal information into four channels. Redundant information R is accessible from either modality. Unique information U_1 and U_2 is accessible only from modality 1 or modality 2. Synergistic information S is accessible only when both modalities are present together. The proposed scaling law writes data loss as a sum of four independent power-law curves. Each curve receives only the relevant data stream: R can be reduced by either modality, U_1 by modality 1 data, U_2 by modality 2 data, and S only by the paired count n_p. This differs from prior L(N, D_1, D_2) forms because it gives paired data its own causal role rather than folding it into modality counts. The experimental protocol is built to isolate this variable. Unpaired examples are represented by a learnable null vector plus a modality-presence bit. At test time, both modalities are always present. Cross-entropy is the main loss, with accuracy checked separately. VQA trains classification heads on top of frozen pretrained embeddings; this setting is dominated by the text modality and is useful for observing how unpaired data helps non-synergistic information. NLVR2 finetunes a pretrained multimodal transformer on a task where mutual information is largely synergistic and unimodal models remain near chance. Across settings, the authors sweep total data D, compute budget C, paired count n_p, and multiple random seeds. They count D as D_1 + D_2, the sum of unique examples per modality. As p approaches 1, the number of unique rows decreases; training steps are fixed, so fully paired data sees more epochs but the same number of gradient updates. This counting convention favors unpaired data, making improvements from higher p more attributable to pairing itself. The main findings are consistent: pairing ratio has a large effect on loss; laws without p cannot capture the observed curves; only paired data reduces synergistic loss; unpaired data reduces redundant or unimodal loss only up to the relevant floors; and synergy shows a threshold-like acquisition pattern. Inputs are sampled from an isotropic Gaussian and RMS-normalized, mirroring hidden states before an LM head. A fixed teacher matrix produces hard one-hot labels from the argmax of its softmax output. The student learns with different optimizers. The setup preserves the key nonlinearity behind peaked distribution learning: reducing loss requires both growing the student weight norm, which sharpens the output distribution, and aligning the student direction with the teacher. The analysis decomposes the loss into a radial channel, controlled by norm growth and softmax saturation, and a tangential channel, controlled by directional misalignment. These channels decay with exponents α_r and α_t. SGD places both near one third. Adam produces a different dynamic regime, with α_r near one half and α_t near zero. Second is MultiTalkBench, an interactive benchmark for end-to-end speech-to-speech systems. It jointly evaluates three axes: long conversations beyond ten minutes with probes for entity tracking and topic coherence, one-model-many-user interaction with metrics for addressee selection and turn-taking, and English-Chinese bilingual ability. This differs from prior long-audio benchmarks, which mostly test passive understanding rather than interactive generation, and from prior speech-to-speech benchmarks, which are usually short and dyadic.

Third is a bilingual Moshi-style full-duplex model trained on the new corpus. The paper stays within the end-to-end unified modeling paradigm rather than reverting to an ASR→LLM→TTS pipeline. For pretraining researchers, the main question is how changing the training distribution changes behavior: with both input and output represented in codec-token space, long context, multi-party interaction, and bilingual switching become part of the language modeling objective itself rather than external modules.62:T469,The strongest asset is the released 57.6k-hour synthetic training corpus, which the authors claim exceeds the combined size of prior open full-duplex speech corpora. On the model side, they train a bilingual Moshi-style full-duplex system and report substantial gains over open baselines including Moshi, MiniCPM-o-4.5, and Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct on MultiTalkBench. The excerpt provided does not include the full result tables, but the introduction makes clear that evaluation spans long-horizon interaction, multi-party interaction, and bilingual conversation rather than only short-turn fluency.

When reading the full paper, three result types are worth prioritizing. First, scaling behavior: whether long-context and multi-party abilities improve smoothly with more synthetic data. Second, data-component ablations: what happens when overlap, addressee shifts, memory conditioning, or bilingual mixing are removed. Third, attribution of gains: whether improvements come mainly from corpus scale, richer interaction structure, or model changes. For audio LM work, those are more informative than a single aggregate score.63:T420,The central mechanism is ResearchSpec, a compact executable specification of what the final report must establish. Multiple Planning Writers independently search and read sources, then propose candidate structures. A Planning Judge consolidates them, a Critic looks for missing questions and cases, and a Reviser folds the feedback back into the specification. ResearchSpec stores each section’s scope, research questions, required entities or cases, provisional source leads, and hierarchical section IDs. Validators check ID uniqueness, parent-child consistency, consecutive ordering, and required fields before dispatch. Each Researcher then receives the full ResearchSpec plus one section assignment, conducts further evidence gathering in an independent context, and writes a complete section. The assembled draft is reviewed by a Global Editor, while Local Editors apply targeted revisions to affected sections. The design trades some flexibility for controllability: the plan is refined before dispatch and then held fixed during section research.64:T445,The central concept is strategic diversity: substantive variation in how a problem is approached, not lexical variation or embedding-space distance. The paper proposes two ways to generate strategically diverse self-training data using the model itself. The first adapts Verbalized Sampling: the model lists multiple possible approaches with estimated probabilities, and each approach is then used as a hidden instruction for generating a full response. The second method, Groot, asks the model to build a hierarchical decision tree over approaches and samples distinct root-to-leaf paths. This is natural for competitive programming, where solutions branch by algorithm, data structure, and implementation choices. For story planning, where narrative decisions are interdependent and less hierarchical, the unstructured VS-style approach is more suitable. Compared with high-temperature IID sampling, both methods force the model to commit to different approaches before producing the final answer, so they change the strategy distribution rather than only perturbing token-level realization.65:T893,FROST has two main ingredients: real-anchored utility estimation and conditional filtering.

For utility estimation, each training step draws both a real batch and a synthetic batch. The method maintains an exponential moving average of gradients from recent real batches, which serves as a smoothed reference direction for the real-data objective. Each synthetic sample is then scored by the alignment between its gradient and this real-gradient reference. The intuition is straightforward: if a synthetic sample pushes parameters in a direction similar to what recent real data prefers, it is more likely to be useful; if it points away, it is more likely to be harmful or off-distribution.

The second ingredient is conditional filtering. The authors argue that per-sample gradient utility is noisy, so filtering every batch aggressively can remove useful supervision. They first aggregate utilities at the batch level and compare the batch mean against recent history to determine whether the batch falls inside a moderate utility band. Batches inside the band are kept as-is. Only out-of-band batches trigger sample-level filtering, where interquartile-range thresholds are used to retain or discard examples within the batch. This design is meant to avoid overreacting to stochastic gradient noise while still rescuing good samples from otherwise weak batches.

Relative to common synthetic-data selection methods, FROST differs in three ways. It does not require a separate pretrained feature extractor for fidelity/diversity scoring, so it avoids expensive offline preprocessing of the full synthetic pool. It does not need a held-out validation set or an external judge, because the real training stream itself provides the anchor. And it is online: utility is recomputed as the model evolves, rather than assigned once in a static preprocessing stage.

From a pretraining perspective, the hidden assumption is that an EMA of real-data gradients is a stable proxy for the target objective. That seems plausible in moderate-scale fine-tuning, but it is less obvious in large mixed-corpus pretraining where gradient noise, domain conflict, and real/synthetic ratios can be very different.66:T621,The paper evaluates FROST on image classification, LLM fine-tuning for text-to-SQL, and a large industrial ads re-ranking system. On the public benchmarks, it filters out roughly 20% to 30% of synthetic data while outperforming training on the full synthetic pool.

The reported gains are 0.58% to 1.14% absolute accuracy improvement across three synthetic image generators, and 0.9% improvement on text-to-SQL fine-tuning. The industrial result is more telling in practical terms: using the full noisy synthetic pool causes a 0.211% relative NE regression compared with the real-only baseline, while FROST turns that into a 0.096% relative NE improvement. The authors note that gains around 0.02% are already considered meaningful in mature production recommenders, so the industrial effect size is not trivial.

Methodologically, the matched-drop-ratio comparison is important. The paper compares selection methods under the same synthetic-data discard rate, which makes the gains more attributable to better selection rather than simply using less data. Also worth checking is the ablation on batch-level gating plus sample-level filtering versus always-on per-sample filtering, since that is the part intended to control gradient-noise sensitivity.

The main caveat is scope. The LLM experiment is a downstream fine-tuning task, not large-scale language-model pretraining. The paper does not establish that real-anchored gradient utility remains stable or cost-effective for next-token pretraining with large synthetic corpora or reasoning-heavy synthetic mixtures.67:T4d9,For a skim read, start with the Introduction and Method to understand the logic of real-anchored utility and conditional filtering. Then read the text-to-SQL experiment and the main ablations. Around 20 to 30 minutes should be enough to decide whether the idea is portable to your own data pipeline.

Focus on four details. First, inspect how utility is computed in practice: full gradients, projected gradients, or some approximation. That determines scalability. Second, check how the real-gradient EMA is updated and stabilized, because the whole method depends on the anchor being reliable. Third, read the calibration rule for batch means and the IQR-based sample filtering, since that is where the paper tries to avoid over-filtering under noisy gradients. Fourth, look for behavior across different drop ratios, synthetic-data quality levels, and training stages.

If your interest is pretraining data rather than downstream fine-tuning, treat this as a prototype idea: use training signals instead of static data features to select synthetic data. Before scaling it up, the open questions are compute overhead, gradient approximation quality, and whether the real-gradient anchor remains meaningful under multi-domain mixed training.68:T437,The central object is the conditional proof-difficulty function V(T|P), the difficulty of proving a target theorem T given an available premise set P. Lean 4 and mathlib provide the formal environment, and proof difficulty is operationalized through formal proof length or proof cost. Using the dependency structure in mathlib, the authors post-train a 27B model to predict V(T|P) before the proof is actually constructed. They then define intrinsic interestingness as proof length divided by statement length. The intended signal is high information density: a theorem that is short to state but hard to prove is more interesting. They also define utility as the amount by which adding a theorem to the mathematical context compresses later proofs. Utility captures reusable abstraction, while interestingness is easier to estimate locally. The paper reports a strong correlation between the two, which motivates using interestingness as a practical reward. The metric is then used both for post-training theorem generation and for inference-time pruning in recursive discovery.69:T833,The setup is a controlled intervention on teacher-only context. The training data consists of problem-solution pairs. The student always sees only the problem x. The teacher is a frozen copy of the student’s initial checkpoint and provides next-token distributions on the student’s own sampled prefixes. The only thing that changes across runs is the privileged context policy c_l(x) supplied to the teacher.

From the same problem-solution pairs, the authors compile several context levels offline. L1 is the full solution. L2 is a named strategy, giving a method label or strategy cue. L3 is a method-independent framing, which keeps the structural perspective but avoids committing to a specific derivation. L4 is a problem category, an even higher-level abstraction. L5 is answer-only, preserving the destination but removing the path. There is also a control condition that keeps only a fixed 10% prefix of the original solution plus the answer, which helps separate semantic abstraction from simple context shortening. Prompt templates and bridge wording are controlled, and within each model scale the student prompt, rollout procedure, loss, teacher checkpoint, and training set are held fixed.

Two methodological choices are especially important. First, the paper defines context utility by post-training student performance, not by a static property of the teacher distribution. That is the right target for this problem. Second, initial teacher-student KL is treated only as a diagnostic. This allows the authors to test a common intuition—that larger distributional displacement means better teaching—and show that it fails here.

Mechanistically, the difference is easy to state. A full solution gives the teacher one concrete derivation, so when the student deviates from that path the teacher may push probability mass back toward the reference trajectory. Abstract context keeps information about what kind of solution is appropriate while relaxing how it should be reached. In on-policy distillation, that changes the shape of the supervision signal, not just its strength.6a:T79e,The main experiments are on competition mathematics. Students are Qwen3 models at 1.7B, 4B, and 8B. Evaluation includes three in-domain math benchmarks and four transfer benchmarks. Within each scale, the training pipeline is fixed and only the privileged context type changes. Results are reported under multiple rules, including peak mean and endpoint-style summaries, to avoid overfitting conclusions to a single checkpoint selection scheme.

There are three main findings. First, concise intermediate abstractions can outperform full solutions. In the primary runs, the best intermediate context improves in-domain peak mean over the full-solution condition by 1.4 points at 4B and 1.6 points at 8B, while using roughly an order of magnitude fewer hint tokens. Across three seeds, L3 and L4 show positive mean gains over L1 at 4B and 8B under all four reporting rules. Second, answer-only context is surprisingly competitive at larger scales: it comes within 0.2 points of the full-solution condition at 4B and 8B, but trails by 1.76 points at 1.7B. This suggests that as the student becomes stronger, preserving the destination may matter more than exposing a full path. Third, initial KL does not rank teaching utility. Full solutions induce the largest initial teacher-student KL at every scale, yet they do not produce the best trained students at 4B or 8B. Item-level analysis further shows that context changes which problems the student ends up solving, not just the overall average.

A useful robustness check recompiles the abstract contexts with Qwen3-8B and still preserves the peak advantage at larger scales, which argues against the effect being an artifact of one specific offline compiler. The supplementary studies on heterogeneous assignment and learned routing are secondary; the main result already stands: there is no universally best privileged context, and the preferred abstraction level depends on student scale and task.6b:T425,This is a good skim paper, but the framing matters. Start with the introduction, especially the argument that privileged context is part of the supervision mechanism rather than auxiliary metadata. Then read the context taxonomy carefully so that L1 through L5 are clear. After that, go straight to the main result table, focusing on the 4B and 8B comparisons between L3/L4 and L1, and on the answer-only condition staying nearly tied with full solutions. Finish with the KL diagnostic section, which directly challenges the idea that larger teacher-student divergence automatically means better distillation.

If you have about 25 minutes, read in this order: setup figure, context construction section, main table, multi-seed results, KL analysis. The right lens is not “math reasoning method” but “training signal design.” Two questions are worth deeper follow-up: whether the gains come mainly from reducing reference-path bias, and whether the same pattern transfers to reasoning SFT, verifier-guided self-training, or RL-style reasoning pipelines.6c:T7dd,Hill Sampling is intentionally minimal. Start from an initial program x0. At each round, sample N candidate edits from a frozen LLM conditioned on the current incumbent xt. Execute each candidate with the verifier, obtain rewards, and replace the incumbent if the best candidate in the round matches or exceeds the best reward seen so far. The algorithm stores the incumbent’s historical best reward rather than re-evaluating it every round, which is important when execution is stochastic. Equal-reward replacements are allowed to preserve some structural diversity. There is no archive, no crossover, no explicit diversity objective, and no parameter update. The main knobs are decoding temperature, samples per round, and number of rounds.

The paper is stronger because it does not stop at introducing the method. It systematically compares three exploration families. First, repeated sampling, where all generations are drawn independently from the same starting point. Relative to that baseline, Hill Sampling adds exactly one persistent state: the best-so-far program fed back into context. Second, evolution strategies applied directly to LLM weights. The authors build a large-scale ES pipeline and separate standard ES learning from a zero-learning-rate variant that keeps only random weight perturbations. This isolates exploration from learning. Third, they test common add-ons such as diversity encouragement, solution combination, extra exploration mechanisms, and code-execution feedback. The conclusion is that none of these are necessary to obtain strong results in this setting.

Mechanistically, Hill Sampling treats the LLM as a conditional editor rather than a one-shot generator. The incumbent acts as a moving scaffold. Future samples are drawn near the current best program instead of restarting from the original problem statement. That creates a simple local search process in context space, not in parameter space. The paper’s main contribution is showing how far that alone can go.6d:T79c,The evaluation covers three verifiable mathematical optimization problems with three open-weight models: circle packing with gpt-oss-20b, sums/differences of finite sets with OLMo-3.1-32B-Instruct, and Erdős’ minimum-overlap problem with Mistral-Small-3.1-24B-Instruct. The emphasis is practical wall-clock performance, not only sample efficiency.

The headline result is on circle packing: Hill Sampling reaches the best published result in under five hours on eight H100 GPUs. On the Erdős minimum-overlap problem, it surpasses the AlphaEvolve algorithmic-discovery reference within 12 hours. The abstract is truncated, but the body makes the qualitative outcome clear: one new published best result and strong competitive performance on the other tasks.

The ablations are the most informative part. Hill Sampling substantially outperforms repeated sampling, showing that best-so-far conditioning is the main source of gain. Standard ES often improves mean return while reducing maximum return, which directly supports the paper’s framing that mean-oriented updates can be misaligned with discovery objectives. Setting the ES learning rate to zero removes learning but keeps random weight perturbations; this sometimes preserves maximum return better than learned ES, yet still underperforms plain token-sampling randomness from the unperturbed model. That is a useful boundary condition for claims about nearby experts in pretrained weight space: even if such experts exist, searching for them may be less effective than output-space exploration when exact verification is available.

The paper also compares Hill Sampling with N=64 and N=512 under the same total sampling budget, changing the trade-off between more frequent incumbent updates and larger within-round candidate sets. Even without all table values here, the setup is worth attention because it probes whether iterative conditioning matters more than wider one-shot search.6e:T514,For a quick read, focus on three parts. First, the opening motivation where the paper distinguishes maximizing best-found reward from improving average sample quality. That framing explains nearly every later result. Second, the formal definition of Hill Sampling in the methods section, especially the stored incumbent reward, equal-reward acceptance, and the budget-matched N=64 versus N=512 variants. Third, the ES and model-noise comparison, which addresses a broader question than the benchmark itself: should test-time exploration happen in token space or weight space?

If you have 20–30 minutes, read in this order: the main algorithm figure, the primary result tables for the three tasks, the ES comparison plots, then the discussion. The key is not the benchmark details but the way the authors strip a complex discovery pipeline down to one necessary mechanism.

Two points are worth deeper thought. One is whether Hill Sampling depends on the locality and compositionality of program editing; the same recipe may transfer less cleanly to natural-language proofs or unverifiable reasoning. The other is the tension between max return and mean return. That distinction has direct implications for verifier-guided decoding, best-of-N methods, and some RL-style test-time adaptation setups.6f:T485,The technical contribution is a clean training framework rather than a new architecture. The paper keeps architecture, model size, tokenizer, and overall language mixture fixed, while varying two main factors: the L1 identity and the order in which the two languages are presented during pretraining. English is always the L2, and the suite spans 21 L1s. The authors train under five exposure regimes, covering more interleaved versus more staged curricula, at three FineWeb scales: 100M, 2B, and 24B tokens, plus a human-scale 100M condition. A strong design choice is the inclusion of matched monolingual baselines for 20 languages, which helps separate genuine bilingual transfer from simple data-composition effects. Conceptually, the framework unifies structured exposure and sequential bilingual training ideas from earlier work, but treats exposure timing itself as the primary intervention. Evaluation is also broader than perplexity: the main target is psycholinguistic alignment, especially L2 eye-tracking reading times on MECO, with additional probes on cross-lingual structural priming and CEFR-stratified learner-error discrimination on BLiSS.70:T4d9,The most consistent result is that ordered or staged exposure tends to align better with human L2 reading times than fully interleaved training. The paper argues this effect is not explained away by higher overall proficiency or better language balance, which is important because those are the obvious confounds. In other words, the point in training when a language is introduced appears to be a meaningful determinant of human-like L2 processing behavior. A second important finding is that the curriculum effect does not transfer uniformly across tasks. On structural priming and BLiSS learner-error discrimination, balanced exposure is often competitive or even better. So staged curricula seem to shape specific processing dynamics rather than universally improving bilingual competence. In scale terms, the suite includes 285 bilingual and 45 monolingual models across 100M, 2B, and 24B tokens, all with checkpoint trajectories. The paper also compares against larger massively multilingual models and reports that carefully designed bilingual curricula can match or exceed their L2 reading-time alignment under much smaller parameter budgets. For researchers working on scaling and data curricula, that is the most actionable result.71:T424,Read this as an experimental-design paper. Start with the setup sections and verify exactly what is held fixed and what is varied; that is where the credibility of the later claims comes from. Then focus on the exposure-regime definitions, data-scale settings, construction of matched monolingual baselines, and checkpoint release strategy. In the experiments, prioritize the MECO reading-time analysis, since that is the main empirical claim. Pay attention to how the authors rule out alternative explanations such as proficiency and balance. After that, read the structural priming and BLiSS sections to understand where the curriculum effect does and does not generalize. The most useful deeper questions are: whether exposure schedule should be treated as an independent scaling axis, whether early checkpoints reveal transfer-emergence phases, and whether matched monolingual controls can be imported into broader multilingual or continual-pretraining studies. A skim takes about 25–35 minutes; the figures and appendix are where much of the value sits.72:T69a,The method combines paired task synthesis with two-stage post-training. The authors distinguish two safety settings. In environment-risk tasks, the user goal is benign but the interface contains hazards; the correct behavior is safe continuation, not refusal. In explicit-misuse tasks, the goal itself is harmful and should be refused. This distinction is central, because collapsing both into a single refuse/not-refuse label would push the model toward conservative shutdown behavior.

To support this, they introduce SCOPE-Gen, an automated pipeline that starts from normal GUI tasks and injects detectable forbidden events or risky interface elements while preserving the original user goal and completion evaluator. This produces paired tasks and three complementary trajectory types: capability trajectories for ordinary execution, risk-handling trajectories for safe continuation under environmental hazards, and refusal trajectories for harmful goals or no-safe-path cases. The reward is defined as the product of completion reward and safety reward, so full credit requires both successful completion and hazard avoidance.

Training proceeds in two stages. First, joint SFT teaches the model all three behaviors together, establishing a conditional execution policy. Second, capability-oriented online RL further improves task completion while monitoring whether safety is retained. The design choice is deliberate: use supervised data to shape the decision boundary first, then use RL to push capability, rather than expecting RL to discover the right safety-capability tradeoff from scratch. The instantiated model is based on Qwen3.5-9B, and the trajectory dataset is SATraj-OS.73:T510,The main evaluations are on OSWorld for capability and OS-BLIND for attack avoidance. The headline numbers are clear. Capability-only training improves execution but does not reliably induce attack avoidance. After joint capability-safety SFT, SCOPE-SFT reaches 49.72% on OSWorld and 66.30% attack-avoidance on OS-BLIND, with a capability-safety harmonic mean of 56.83%. After subsequent capability-oriented online RL, SCOPE-RL improves OSWorld to 54.17% while retaining 64.30% attack avoidance, yielding the best aggregate score of 58.80%.

The ablations are the most informative part. Refusal trajectories account for most of the gain in attack avoidance on OS-BLIND, meaning that explicit supervision is effective for teaching when to stop. Risk-handling trajectories play a different role: they preserve task utility at comparable attack-avoidance levels by teaching the model to continue safely instead of over-refusing. Together, the two trajectory types produce a more balanced conditional policy.

The broader takeaway from the training path—capability-only, then joint SFT, then capability-oriented RL—is that safety does not emerge automatically from capability optimization, but once a safety-aware boundary is learned, further capability improvement does not necessarily erase it.74:T4c8,The method starts from the geometry of the prediction-loss and predictive-entropy plane. A likelihood-only detector uses a horizontal threshold on loss. This fails when many non-members have low loss because they are predictable. The proposed detector instead uses an inclined boundary by correcting loss with predictive entropy. The resulting score has the algebraic form of Helmholtz free energy: token loss plays the role of an energy term, predictive entropy is the uncertainty term, and a coefficient similar to temperature trades them off, giving a score of the form loss minus an entropy correction before sequence-level aggregation. The theoretical analysis shows that when members and non-members have the same mean predictive entropy, the correction preserves the expected membership gap and its lower bound. When the loss gap and entropy gap are positively correlated, an appropriate correction reduces the variance of the gap while preserving its mean, improving standardized separation. The analysis is also extended to settings with a nonzero mean entropy gap. Compared with reference-model or perturbation-based calibration, ETD uses the target model’s own token-level predictive distribution more directly.75:T43d,The strongest evidence comes from ARC-AGI-3, Frontier-CS polyomino packing, MNIST classifier compression, and Terminal-Bench 2.0. On ARC-AGI-3 with Claude Sonnet 4.6, team@3 matches roughly best@13, and team@5 matches roughly best@33, corresponding to effective multipliers of about 4.3x and 6.6x independent agents. On FT09, single-agent success is 9.4%, while team@3 reaches 90%. On LP85, 64 single-agent trials fail to solve the game, while team@5 succeeds 65% of the time. On Frontier-CS polyomino packing, team@4 scores 0.922 with Claude Opus 4.6 and 0.910 with Sonnet 4.6, compared with 0.893 and 0.891 for the strongest solo runs and 0.894 for the prior best-known result. On MNIST classifier compression, a 96-hour GPT-5.6 Sol team@4 run finds a 1,957-byte classifier at 99.4% accuracy, improving on the 2,461-byte known human solution and single-agent baselines. The negative result on Terminal-Bench 2.0 is important: team@2 improves over one attempt but does not beat independent pass@2, likely because intermediate feedback is not reliable enough to rank partial solutions.76:Tb2f,方法核心是一条多阶段 agentic environment construction pipeline。输入只有源代码仓库本身，不使用任务特定的 issue、PR、文档或人工规格。第一步是功能发现与任务设计。系统让 agent 检查代码结构、构建配置和公共入口，优先选择需要跨文件理解、具有公开接口且行为可观察的功能单元，支持 CLI、纯函数库接口和有状态 API。这里的关键不是简单抽函数，而是挑选“能写成行为规范、又不把实现细节锁死”的目标功能。

第二步是代码库改造。CodeMidas 会把目标功能从原仓库中移除或留空，保留其余项目结构、依赖和上下文，形成 solver 可操作的开发起点。这样做比从零给一个编程题更接近真实软件工作：模型需要在原项目约束下补全缺失实现，而不是在孤立函数上做 HumanEval 式补题。

第三步是基于执行的测试构造。系统运行原始代码，通过执行轨迹、返回值、状态变化、文件输出、CLI 输出等可观察行为来生成测试期望。这里的设计重点是“behavioral specification”而不是“implementation matching”：测试要约束外部行为，但允许不同内部实现。文中明确强调要避免把原实现细节直接编码进 verifier，否则会把任务退化成补全原代码。为此，测试构造结合执行证据、边界情况扩展和一致性检查，尽量让 verifier 接受替代性正确实现。

第四步是环境一致性检查。构造后的环境需要保证：原始正确实现能通过 verifier；移除目标实现后的起始环境不能 trivially 通过；容器化依赖、构建脚本和测试注入流程都稳定。这一步更像数据工程里的 validity gate，避免把噪声环境送进 RL。

第五步是 rollout-based filtering，也是这篇工作最有信息量的部分。作者不是只看静态构造结果，而是先让 agent 在候选环境上 rollout，再用这些 rollout 反过来筛任务。过滤信号包括：对抗性 rollout 检查是否存在泄漏或 reward hacking 路径；solution review 判断 verifier 的通过/失败是否真的符合题意；以及 success rate 统计，用来剔除过难、过易或奖励不稳定的任务。也就是说，任务质量不是由生成器单方面决定，而是由“环境 × agent 行为”共同定义。这比只做静态 test generation 更接近真实 RL 需求。

最终得到的数据集包含 5,545 个可验证任务，来自 3,185 个开源代码库，覆盖 23 种编程语言和 15 个技术领域。训练时使用 GRPO 在 MiMo-V2.5 上做 RL。论文还分析了训练后 agent 行为变化，发现模型会更多探索代码库，并更频繁地执行自写检查，这说明学到的不只是 benchmark-specific patching，而是更一般的工作流策略。77:Ta02,CodeMidas is an agentic pipeline for environment construction. The only task-specific input is a source repository. It does not consume issues, PRs, or human-written specs. First, the system identifies candidate functionality by inspecting repository structure, build metadata, and public entry points. It prioritizes functionality with observable behavior and nontrivial codebase context, including CLI tools, pure library functions, and stateful APIs. The selection criterion is important: the target should admit a behavioral specification while leaving implementation freedom open.

Second, the repository is adapted into a development starting point. The target implementation is removed or blanked out, while the rest of the project structure, dependencies, and surrounding context are preserved. This makes the task closer to real software work than isolated function completion.

Third, CodeMidas constructs tests grounded in execution of the original code. It runs the original implementation and uses observable outputs, return values, state transitions, file effects, and CLI behavior to infer expected behavior. The design goal is behavioral verification rather than implementation matching. The verifier should reject wrong solutions but still accept alternative correct implementations, so the pipeline tries to avoid overfitting tests to the original code path.

Fourth, the environment is checked for execution consistency. The original implementation must pass; the stripped starting point must not pass trivially; the containerized dependencies and grading flow must be stable. This is a data validity gate more than a modeling contribution, but it is essential for RL.

Fifth, and most interestingly, the paper adds rollout-based filtering. Candidate environments are probed with agent rollouts before RL training. The pipeline uses adversarial rollouts to detect leakage and exploitability, solution reviews to assess whether verifier outcomes align with the stated requirements, and rollout success rates to remove tasks that are too noisy, too easy, too hard, or reward-misaligned. This is a strong design choice: task quality is defined not only statically, but through interaction with actual agent behavior.

The final dataset contains 5,545 verifiable tasks from 3,185 open-source repositories, spanning 23 programming languages and 15 technical domains. RL is then run with GRPO on MiMo-V2.5. The paper also studies behavioral changes during training, showing increased repository exploration and more self-written checks by the agent.78:T56c,The constructed dataset has 5,545 tasks from 3,185 repositories, covering 23 languages and 15 domains. MiMo-V2.5 is trained with GRPO on these environments. The trained policy improves on all five external benchmarks. Reported headline numbers include DeepSWE pass rate rising from 10.0% to 21.7%, ProgramBench Almost Solved increasing from 4.5 to 21.5, and Terminal-Bench v2.1 pass rate improving from 63.7% to 72.2%. The gains span issue repair, whole-program construction, code translation, and terminal interaction, which suggests transfer beyond the exact training distribution.

The scale-versus-quality study is more informative than the benchmark table alone. Increasing the number of high-quality tasks from 1k to 3k to 5,545 yields progressively better results on SWE-bench Pro, DeepSWE, and CodeMidas Val. That is a strong signal that verifier reliability and environment curation matter more than naive expansion.

The behavioral analysis is also useful. As RL progresses, agents explore repositories more and perform more varied self-verification. Agent-written checks correlate with higher success rates, and similar behavior shifts appear on external tasks. These are softer signals than pass rate, but they help explain what the policy is learning.79:T4e1,For a skim-level read, focus on the motivation and the construction pipeline. Questions worth keeping in mind while reading: how much of the verifier is truly behavioral rather than implementation-specific; whether rollout-based filtering biases the task distribution toward the current agent’s competence; and whether this pipeline could generalize to broader agent environments beyond coding.7a:T47a,The authors build a controlled pretraining setup using a Fictional Knowledge Dataset with 2,048 synthetic facts about invented entities and attributes. Each fact is rendered into diverse documents across languages for injection during pretraining, with held-out multiple-choice questions for evaluation. For a fact, the authors know exactly how many times it appeared in language A and language B. They then regress target-language accuracy on native and foreign exposure counts. The ratio between the foreign-exposure coefficient and the native-exposure coefficient defines CL_eq. A score of 100% means that one exposure in the foreign language is as useful as one exposure in the target language; 0% means no effective transfer. To remove natural-language confounds, the paper also evaluates cloned language copies that are structurally identical but occupy different token spaces. This isolates vocabulary separation from syntax or semantics. The main intervention, word-wise translation, is motivated by this mechanism: it tries to unify token spaces for otherwise vocabulary-disjoint languages rather than relying on post-training alignment.7b:T426,The experiments pretrain bilingual models from scratch while injecting fictional facts at controlled rates. The dataset validation shows chance-level MCQ accuracy with zero injection and a roughly log-shaped improvement as injected paraphrases increase, confirming that the facts are learnable and exposure-controlled.
